title: Sarajevo Records Its Arms-Embargo Posture
sources: UNSCR 713 (25 September 1991) — comprehensive arms embargo on former Yugoslavia
content:
The UNSCR 713 arms embargo of September 1991 applied uniformly to all of former Yugoslavia — and, in the Bosnian government's view, asymmetrically. The VRS inherited the JNA's artillery, armour, and ammunition stocks; the HVO drew on Croatian state supply across the airbridge; the ARBiH, raised from a republic with little heavy-weapons industry, was left rifle-poor against both. The embargo froze that disparity in place.

Throughout 1993 Izetbegović argued the case directly — to the UN General Assembly and to the US Congress — that the embargo privileged the aggressor it was meant to restrain. Prime Minister Haris Silajdžić ran a parallel shuttle-diplomacy circuit pressing the same point in Western capitals. The advocacy was a defining diplomatic posture: it framed Sarajevo as the victim of a structurally unjust constraint and sought to convert that framing into either a formal lift or de facto relief.

The choice was not only rhetorical. Pressing for a lift while striking on the ground aligned diplomacy with military pressure; seeking clandestine arms accepted the embargo's persistence while circumventing it, as the Iran-Croatia channel and the "black flights" later did; abandoning the advocacy conceded the constraint; accepting the embargo outright would have meant fighting within it indefinitely. Historically Sarajevo pursued the lift advocacy publicly while tolerating clandestine resupply — a dual posture that the US "green light" of 1994 partly legitimized.

The posture recorded here conditions the ARBiH's material trajectory and Sarajevo's standing as the war's designated victim in Western opinion.
